items.name: UK AI White Paper — 5 Principles
items.description: AI White Paper pro-innovation approach: five cross-sector principles that regulators are asked to apply to AI without new legislation

titles.text: Cross-sector principles for the regulation of AI

requirements.text: AI should be safe, transparent and controllable, with systems designed for safety, security and robustness, appropriate fail-safes and the ability for humans to intervene.
requirements.rationale: Regulators expect safety properties to be engineered, not assumed.

controls.description: Design fail-safe and human-intervention paths into AI systems proportionate to their risk.

requirements.text: Organisations should be able to explain what AI is doing and take responsibility for it, with transparent processes and clear accountability mechanisms in place.

controls.description: Record accountable owners for each AI system and the explanations available to affected parties.

requirements.text: AI systems should be fair and just, with attention to bias, discrimination and equitable treatment across different groups in design, data and outcomes.
requirements.rationale: Fairness must be evidenced across the groups a system touches.

controls.description: Test outputs for disparate impact across protected characteristics and document remediation where found.

requirements.text: Organisations should be transparent about when AI is being used, how decisions are made and the limitations of AI systems, and be able to explain what the AI is doing.

controls.description: Disclose AI use and provide accessible explanations of decision logic and system limitations to users.

requirements.text: There should be appropriate redress and challenge mechanisms so individuals can contest AI-driven decisions and access meaningful human review.
requirements.rationale: Contestability is the principle that makes the other four reviewable in practice.

controls.description: Operate a documented route for contesting AI-driven decisions with human review by a competent person.
Track contest volumes, outcomes and changes made in response.
